title: America’s Samurai Myth
gist: Jeremy Shapiro (ECFR) argues Obama's 2013 Syria red-line reversal was a diplomatic triumph that removed 1,308 tons of chemical agent, while Trump's 2017 Tomahawk strike achieved nothing, and that Washington's reputation-based theory of credibility makes force cheap and diplomacy expensive, currently keeping the US in a 'pointless war' with Iran.

insights.claim: Faced with a credible US threat in 2013, Assad surrendered nearly his entire chemical arsenal: inspectors removed 1,308 tons of agent and precursor from an active war zone by June 2014.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Threat-backed diplomacy can deliver concrete disarmament outcomes that strikes cannot.
insights.quote: Inspectors hauled 1,308 tons of agent and precursor out of an active war zone. They finished the job by June 2014.

insights.claim: The red line episode was a triumph of US diplomacy, not a credibility failure; the consensus view held even by Panetta, Hagel and Rice is wrong.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Challenges the dominant establishment narrative that shapes escalation decisions.
insights.quote: The red line incident is in fact a triumph of American diplomacy, a shining island of U.S. diplomatic wisdom amid a sea of stupid wars.
insights.locator: The only problem with this consensus

insights.claim: Russia, wanting to avoid US intervention, had to pressure Assad hard and make continued Russian protection conditional on giving up the chemical stockpile, which Damascus saw as its poor man's deterrent against Israel.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Great-power patrons can be leveraged to extract concessions when they fear US intervention.
insights.locator: We should understand what that meant

insights.claim: Removing the stockpile likely saved tens of thousands of lives given later regime desperation in 2015 and 2024, at zero casualties and zero munitions.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Counterfactual valuation of diplomacy versus force.
insights.quote: But any sober estimate of the lives that the deal saved runs into the tens of thousands.

insights.claim: In 2013 the US had no military option to destroy Syria's chemical arsenal; bombing stockpiles risked a lethal cloud and Pentagon estimates for securing sites by force ran past 75,000 troops.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Shows the limits of air power against WMD stockpiles, relevant to Iran-style targets.
insights.locator: Pentagon planners designed the strike package

insights.claim: Trump's April 2017 strike of 59 Tomahawks after Khan Shaykhun prevented no chemical attacks and changed no Syrian calculation; aircraft flew from the base the next day and Assad gassed Douma a year later.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Punitive strikes have weak deterrent effect; markets should not price them as regime-changing.
insights.quote: Syrian aircraft flew from that field again the next day.

insights.claim: The deal's gaps (omitted material, chlorine use, retained sarin) indict the military alternative more, since a strike would have left both the hidden residue and the 1,308 tons removed.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Compare policy options against realistic alternatives, not perfection.
insights.locator: Of course, the deal was incomplete.

insights.claim: Political science finds little evidence that adversaries keep a ledger of a leader's past resolve; credibility is local, judged on interests and capabilities in the case at hand.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Reputation-based escalation arguments, a common geopolitical risk driver, rest on weak evidence.
insights.quote: scholars find that a country’s credibility is quite local

insights.claim: Russia seized Crimea because Yanukovych fled Kyiv and its Sevastopol fleet sat in a country turning west, not because Obama declined to bomb Damascus; Russia also dismembered Georgia in 2008 under a president who had invaded two countries.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Adversary behavior is driven by local stakes; forecast conflicts on those, not on US 'resolve' signals.

insights.claim: Washington scores foreign policy by presidential reputation, judged by eagerness to use force, making it practically the only metric of success.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Explains a structural bias toward military action in US policy.
insights.locator: But reputational arguments have huge currency

insights.claim: In the days after the 2017 strike, the five top US newspapers ran 18 editorials and op-eds about it and none opposed it.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Media incentives reward visible force, reinforcing escalation bias.
insights.quote: the five top American newspapers ran 18 editorials and op-eds about it, and not one of them opposed it.

insights.claim: A scoring system that rewards ordnance and ignores outcomes makes violence cheap and diplomacy expensive, and presidents including Trump can do that math.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Expect persistent bias toward kinetic options in crises.
insights.quote: a political scoring system that rewards ordnance and ignores outcomes makes violence cheap and diplomacy expensive.

insights.claim: Allies weaponize the credibility frame in US domestic debate: Gulf states wanted the US to remove Assad, and Morawiecki and Stoltenberg linked Ukraine's outcome to a Chinese invasion of Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Allied lobbying framed as credibility tests should be discounted as interest-driven.

insights.claim: Commentators and Adm. Samuel Paparo argue fighting Iran is needed to prove the US will defend Taiwan, which the author treats as the same flawed credibility logic.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Links Middle East war persistence to Indo-Pacific signaling narratives.

insights.claim: The establishment teaches presidents to make cheap commitments and bills them later; Obama's error was blurting an unconsidered threat, not restraint.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Loose rhetorical commitments create later escalation pressure.
insights.quote: He won the war but lost the press conference.

insights.claim: The red line 'samurai myth' that a drawn sword must taste blood is being used to promote war with Iran, e.g., FDD urging Trump to enforce his Iran red line.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Signals a sticky escalation narrative sustaining the Iran conflict.
insights.quote: A U.S. military sword once unsheathed must taste blood or the nation loses its honor.
insights.locator: The red line incident, to mangle

insights.claim: Trump's attachment to a macho code and fear of looking weak by abandoning force options appear to be keeping the US in a pointless war in Iran.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Suggests the Iran war may be prolonged by political rather than strategic logic, extending energy and geopolitical risk.
insights.quote: Trump’s attachment to this macho code and his fear of looking weak by abandoning force options in Iran seems to be keeping him (and us) in a pointless war.
insights.locator: The lesson for the war in Iran

insights.claim: Negotiation, a limited settlement, or declaring victory and going home may deliver more than further strikes in Iran.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Off-ramp scenarios remain viable if political framing shifts.
insights.locator: The lesson for the war in Iran
